index ffac5ce22e60816f18267d742455e4936b6d1c1a..1b0f5dcba15800dac0be69882c7770939fe624ce 100644
--- a/inflection/__init__.py
+++ b/inflection/__init__.py
@@ -9,6 +9,7 @@
 
     :license: MIT, see LICENSE for more details.
 """
+import itertools
 import re
 import typing
 import unicodedata
@@ -360,6 +361,10 @@ def titleize(word: str) -> str:
     create a nicer looking title. :func:`titleize` is meant for creating pretty
     output.
 
+    Words written entirely in capitals, such as acronyms, are kept exactly as
+    written. The exception is a string without any lowercase letters: it is
+    taken to be shouted and is title-cased like any other.
+
     Examples::
 
       >>> titleize("man from the boondocks")
@@ -370,13 +375,64 @@ def titleize(word: str) -> str:
       'The Man Without A Past'
       >>> titleize("raiders_of_the_lost_ark")
       'Raiders Of The Lost Ark'
+      >>> titleize("NASA rocket launch")
+      'NASA Rocket Launch'
+      >>> titleize("parseHTTPResponse")
+      'Parse HTTP Response'
+      >>> titleize("HELLO WORLD")
+      'Hello World'
 
     """
-    return re.sub(
+    title = re.sub(
         r"\b('?\w)",
         lambda match: match.group(1).capitalize(),
         humanize(underscore(word)).title()
     )
+    if not any(char.islower() for char in word):
+        return title
+    return _restore_uppercase_words(title, _split_words(word))
+
+
+def _restore_uppercase_words(title: str, separated: str) -> str:
+    """
+    Put the words of ``separated`` that are written entirely in capitals back
+    into ``title``, the result of lowercasing ``separated`` and title-casing
+    it the way :func:`titleize` does.
+
+    Title-casing only changes the case of words, replaces separators and may
+    drop a trailing ``"id"`` word (see :func:`humanize`), so the n-th word of
+    ``title`` is the n-th word of ``separated`` with its case changed.
+    """
+    originals = (run for is_word, run in _word_runs(separated) if is_word)
+    restored: typing.List[str] = []
+    for is_word, run in _word_runs(title):
+        if is_word:
+            original = next(originals, '')
+            if original.isupper():
+                run = original
+        restored.append(run)
+    return ''.join(restored)
+
+
+def _word_runs(string: str) -> typing.Iterator[typing.Tuple[bool, str]]:
+    """
+    Split a string into maximal runs of word characters (letters, combining
+    marks, numbers and any other character that has a case, such as ``ⓐ``)
+    and of separators, yielding ``(is_word, run)`` pairs.
+
+    Changing the case of a character never turns it into a separator or the
+    other way round, so a string and any case-converted form of it have the
+    same runs.
+    """
+    def is_word_char(char: str) -> bool:
+        return (
+            unicodedata.category(char)[0] in 'LMN'
+            or char.isupper()
+            or char.islower()
+        )
+
+    for is_word, chars in itertools.groupby(string, is_word_char):
+        yield is_word, ''.join(chars)
 
 
 def transliterate(string: str) -> str:
@@ -412,11 +468,25 @@ def underscore(word: str) -> str:
         >>> camelize(underscore("IOError"))
         'IoError'
 
+    """
+    return _split_words(word).lower()
+
+
+def _split_words(word: str) -> str:
+    """
+    Separate the words of a CamelCased or dasherized expression with
+    underscores, leaving the case of every letter as it is. This is
+    :func:`underscore` without the final lowercasing.
+
+    Example::
+
+        >>> _split_words("HTMLTidy-generator")
+        'HTML_Tidy_generator'
+
     """
     word = re.sub(r"([A-Z]+)([A-Z][a-z])", r'\1_\2', word)
     word = re.sub(r"([a-z\d])([A-Z])", r'\1_\2', word)
-    word = word.replace("-", "_")
-    return word.lower()
+    return word.replace("-", "_")

description: Keeps the legacy titleize pipeline, then (only if the input has a lowercase letter) aligns its words one-to-one with the case-preserved camel-split input (underscore refactored into _split_words().lower()) via a case-invariant letter/mark/number tokenizer and puts back every word that is str.isupper().
